title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Introduction
content: Cholinergic toxicity is caused by medications, drugs, and substances that stimulate, enhance, or mimic the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Acetylcholine is the primary neurotransmitter of the parasympathetic nervous system. Acetylcholine stimulates muscarinic and nicotinic receptors to cause muscle contraction and glandular secretions. Cholinergic toxicity occurs when too much acetylcholine is present in the receptor synapse, leading to excessive parasympathetic effects.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Etiology
content: Cholinergic toxicity may result from insecticides, nerve agents, medications, and mushrooms. The most common cause of cholinergic toxicity worldwide is exposure to organophosphate and carbamate insecticides. Exposure to these insecticides may occur through inhalation of vapors, ingestion, or direct contact with the chemical on the skin or mucous membranes.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Etiology
content: Sarin gas is a nerve gas typically seen in chemical warfare. Sarin gas was initially made in Germany in 1938 as a pesticide. It is well known for being involved in terrorist attacks in Japan in 1994 and 1995.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Etiology
content: Cholinergic drugs may cause a cholinergic crisis during clinical use or after an overdose. These drugs include medications used to treat myasthenia gravis, such as edrophonium and neostigmine, as well as pilocarpine used for glaucoma. Additionally, Alzheimer drugs like rivastigmine and donepezil are also included. Essentially, any agent that creates an abundance of acetylcholine at the synapse may cause cholinergic toxicity. These drugs may cause weakness, but a cholinergic crisis is very rare with drugs taken at therapeutic doses.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: Organophosphates have been used worldwide for over 50 years as insecticides, though usage has decreased in the past 10 to 20 years. There are about 3000000 exposures to organophosphates or carbamates worldwide each year, with approximately 200000 fatalities as a result of exposure. [1] One million of these exposures were found to be unintentional, while the other 2 million exposures were secondary to suicidal attempts. [2] The American Association of Poison Control Centers reported 86914 human exposures to pesticides in the United States in 1996 alone. [3] Poisoning due to occupational exposure only accounted for one-fifth of the incidental contact, with a fatality rate of less than 1%. More than 90% of the non-occupational incidents were intentional, with a fatality rate exceeding 10%. Accidental exposure accounted for the other 10% with homicidal use less than 1%.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: The underlying mechanism for cholinergic toxicity is excessive stimulation of cholinergic receptors, which can be caused by substances that mimic, stimulate, or enhance acetylcholine. The symptom complex produced by the agent depends on what type of receptor or combination of receptors is activated. There are three types of cholinergic receptors: central, muscarinic, and nicotinic. Excess acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors will result in symptoms of increased secretions, bronchoconstriction, bradycardia, vomiting, and abdominal cramping. Excess acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors can cause muscle fasciculations or paralysis due to the activation of the neuromuscular junction. Excess acetylcholine in the central nervous system can cause confusion, headaches, or drowsiness. [1]

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Physical exam findings depend on which receptors experience accumulation of acetylcholine. Acetylcholine accumulation at muscarinic receptors produces an increase in secretions, which can manifest as bronchorrhea, salivation, tearing, and sweating, bronchoconstriction, chest tightness, wheezing, bradycardia, vomiting, increased gastrointestinal motility, abdominal tightness, diarrhea, and cramps. Activation of muscarinic receptors in the eye by excess acetylcholine will produce miosis and blurry vision. Increased acetylcholine at nicotinic sites at the neuromuscular junction causes muscle fasciculations and flaccid paralysis due to excess acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. Excess acetylcholine in the brains of patients may cause headache, insomnia, giddiness, confusion, and drowsiness. More severe exposures may cause central depression, resulting in slurred speech, convulsions, coma, and respiratory depression. Death can occur due to effects on the heart, respiration, and brain.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: The correct diagnosis for cholinergic toxicity hinges on the ability to recognize the clinical picture and connect it with the history that would make this toxidrome possible. A thorough history and physical is critical in making this diagnosis. If the toxidrome is present, it is essential to try to identify the agent, as the effects and length of toxicity vary by agent.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: There is no specific laboratory or radiographic testing that will definitively make the diagnosis. RBC acetylcholinesterase levels can be measured, but most hospital laboratories do not offer this test.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Evaluation and management of every patient should begin with ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure). Usual airway and circulatory support are necessary with two exceptions. During intubation, succinylcholine should not be used because the lack of acetylcholinesterase caused by the poisoning will cause prolonged paralysis. Aggressive decontamination is necessary. All clothing should be removed and discarded. The skin and eyes should be washed to avoid continued absorption of the agent. Healthcare workers should wear protective gear to prevent dermal and inhalation exposure to the agent.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Once suspected, treatment should consist of IV administration of atropine and pralidoxime. Atropine is given first, as pralidoxime may transiently worsen symptoms. Atropine acts as a direct physiological antidote by antagonizing the actions of excessive acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors, thereby preventing symptoms such as bronchorrhea, bradycardia, salivation, and bronchoconstriction. Atropine can cross the blood-brain barrier and can help decrease the activity of centrally acting excess acetylcholine. The initial dose of IV atropine is 2 to 5 mg in adults and 0.05 mg/kg in children every 5 minutes until pulmonary symptoms improve. Atropine must be titrated to alleviate bronchorrhea and bronchospasm; this may require large doses of atropine, and treatment may continue for several days. The hospital pharmacy should receive advance notice that an extra atropine supply may be necessary.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Because atropine does not bind to nicotinic receptors, it does not treat neuromuscular dysfunction. Oximes such as pralidoxime have three actions that show benefit in acute cholinergic toxicity. Pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase, provides endogenous anticholinergic effects, and detoxifies unbound organophosphates. Oximes are used to act on the nicotinic neuromuscular junction. They should therefore be administered when signs of muscle weakness are present, especially if the weakness is affecting the respiratory system. [4] Most patients with organophosphate poisoning require treatment with an oxime; this is due to the variability of responses to oximes and the possibility of delayed toxicity. The FDA-approved dosage of pralidoxime for organophosphate toxicity is 1 to 2 g infusion over 30 minutes, which may be repeated in one hour if muscle weakness persists. A continuous infusion may also be necessary after the bolus dose is administered. If available, obtain a toxicology or poison center consultation.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Many diseases and toxicities can mimic cholinergic toxicity. These include carbamate toxicity, nicotinic toxicity, carbachol, methacholine, bethanechol, or pilocarpine overdose, pyridostigmine toxicity, neostigmine toxicity, mushroom poisoning, myasthenia gravis, Eaton-Lambert syndrome, Guillain-Barré syndrome, botulism, opioid overdose, sepsis, toxic alcohol ingestions, severe asthma exacerbation, and severe gastroenteritis.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: Medical management may be difficult in cholinergic toxicity, and thus, the fatality rate is generally more than 15%. [6]

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Complications
content: Because cholinergic toxicity involves the parasympathetic nervous system, many severe complications can occur. Due to severe bronchospasm and bronchorrhea, the respiratory system may fail, requiring assisted ventilation. Respiratory failure may also arise from profound muscle weakness that can affect the muscles of the diaphragm. The cardiovascular system may collapse due to profound bradycardia, hypotension, hypertension, or arrhythmias, which can accelerate in a patient with known coronary artery disease, known chronic heart failure, or other cardiovascular diseases. These effects on the cardiovascular and respiratory systems may result in cardiopulmonary arrest and death. Electrolyte abnormalities may also result from excessive vomiting and diarrhea associated with cholinergic toxicity, putting the patient at risk of arrhythmias and death.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients who may come into contact with insecticides or pesticides require education in the proper handling and care of such substances. Correct handling procedures can decrease occupational exposure to this chemical and, therefore, reduce the number of incidents worldwide. [7]

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Key points to consider regarding cholinergic toxicity are as follows: Cholinergic toxicity may occur with the use of pesticides or medications; however, most serious exposures are due to organophosphate or carbamate pesticide exposure. This poisoning kills about 200,000 people worldwide, especially in the Asia-Pacific region. Diagnosis is made by recognizing the cholinergic toxidrome when it is suspected based on the history of illness. Toxicity may be immediate or delayed. Treatment is aggressive supportive care, plus targeted therapy for cholinergic toxicity: atropine followed by an available oxime such as pralidoxime. Decontamination and personal protective equipment must be used to prevent further absorption of the agent by the patient and to protect caregivers from harm. Consultation with a toxicologist or poison center is recommended.

title: Cholinergic Toxicity(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The most challenging aspect of treating cholinergic toxicity is the initial recognition of the disease process, which would allow for prompt treatment and, therefore, better outcomes. Nurses and physicians should educate patients about pesticide exposures and how to recognize the symptoms. Strict decontamination policies can help reduce inadvertent exposure to nurses and healthcare workers in the emergency department. Reducing the use of pesticides worldwide may help decrease the number of cases of accidental toxicity resulting from occupational exposure. Pharmacists should review the patient's medication record to verify that there are no medications that could result in cholinergic toxicity or exacerbate existing toxicity. Treatment of cholinergic toxicity requires an interprofessional team approach that includes physicians, nurses, pharmacists, poison control experts, and toxicologists to ensure optimal patient care and outcomes.
